title: How to Introduce Herbs and Spices to Babies
summary: Can we add herbs and spices to food for babies? Pediatric dietitian Marina Chaparro, MPH, RDN, CDCES helps us explain the when, what, and how.
body_markdown:
*This blog is for informational purposes only and does not provide medical advice; see our[full disclaimer](https://onceuponafarmorganics.com/pages/blog-disclaimer) for more information.*


Herbs and spices are such a big part of the food we eat. They can add subtle enhancements or really transform a dish. Knowing what’s ahead, we can help prepare babies for the wonderful world of flavor by (gently) spicing up the food they eat. Let’s talk when, what, and how.


## When can babies safely start having herbs and spices?


From the beginning! “Babies can safely begin having herbs and spices around 6 months, once they’re developmentally ready to start solids,” says pediatric dietitian[Marina Chaparro, MPH, RDN, CDCES](https://onceuponafarmorganics.com/blogs/upon-a-blog/marina-chaparro) . If your baby is showing readiness for solids (good head and neck control, sitting with support, and interest in food), they’re also ready to begin exploring flavor.


As you start introducing them to solid foods, you can introduce them to flavors your family enjoys right alongside them. Herbs and spices can help expand their palate and make foods more interesting. Try simple, mild flavors like cinnamon, garlic, thyme, rosemary, or ginger.


*Introduce your baby to a world of flavor with lightly seasoned frozen Meal Starters.*

## Why Early Exposure to Flavors Matters


There’s a developmental period typically between 6–18 months when babies are especially open to new flavors—this is known as the taste window. “The more variety babies experience during this time,” Chaparro explains, “the more likely they are to accept those foods later on.”


Research shows that[taste preferences begin forming in the first two years of life](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30865953/) , so early exposure can have a lasting impact. And it’s not just flavor either. Variety in textures and types of foods can help encourage more flexibility and curiosity as they grow and try more foods.


## The Best Starter Spices


The best spice to start with depends on your culture, cuisine, and what you’re cooking. Chaparro recommends not shying away from flavor and adapting your current meals rather than creating new ones. “It reduces stress and helps babies grow up experiencing the same foods and flavors as the rest of the family,” she says, “just prepared in a safe, age-appropriate way.”


So, start with what you have in your kitchen. Be sure to keep flavors mild and avoid added salt, sugar, or overly spicy heat.


*Related Reading:[Baby-Friendly Herbs and Spices](https://onceuponafarmorganics.com/blogs/upon-a-blog/baby-friendly-herbs-and-spices)*


## Tips for Safely Introducing Spices


Everything is new to babies, which means they don’t need much seasoning for food to be flavorful. “They’re often very sensitive to even small amounts,” Chaparro says, “so a little truly goes a long way.”


While herbs and spices are generally not considered common allergens, and since they’re typically used in small amounts, the risk is low. “That said,” she continues, “reactions can still happen, so it’s always a good idea to introduce new spices thoughtfully.”


One recommendation for introducing spices is to add them to foods your baby already tolerates well. If there is a reaction, you can more easily identify the cause. You don’t need to wait several days between introducing different flavors; it is helpful to do this one at a time and be mindful of how the baby responds. “Start small, keep it simple, and build from there,” she advises. “Over time, these small exposures can help expand your baby’s palate in a safe and positive ways.”


## Ingredients to Avoid


Avoid added salt or sugar* in the first year of life. This includes salt-based seasonings like garlic salt, onion salt, or flavored blends. “Avoid strong, spicy heat or heavily seasoned foods,” Chaparro shares, “and introduce one new flavor at a time while observing how your baby responds.” This helps build your baby’s palate without relying on added salt or sugar.


**This includes natural options like maple syrup and honey. Honey, in particular, is not safe for infants under 12 months old,[due to the risk of infant botulism](https://publications.aap.org/aapnews/news/13225/Remind-families-honey-can-cause-infant-botulism) .*


## Simple Ways to Add Herbs and Spices to Homemade or Store-Bought Baby Foods


The best way to add herbs and spices to your baby’s food is to build on foods you’re already serving. Chaparro loves adding cinnamon and a touch of vanilla to naturally sweet foods like oatmeal, apples, or banana purées. “It enhances flavor without needing added sugar.” She also encourages playful, familiar combinations like mint and basil with fruit for an unexpected pairing.


For savory foods, think about what you already cook at home. For her kiddos, Chaparro would add fresh herbs like cilantro, rosemary, mint, or basil to fish and meats, along with a drizzle of olive oil to keep things soft and moist. Spices like turmeric and ginger are also great, versatile options. They work well in purées, lentils, beans, or even mashed sweet potatoes.


*Start exploring flavors with ready-to-cook meals, gently flavored with herbs and spices.*


## FAQs


### When can I start giving my baby herbs and spices?


Most babies can begin exploring herbs and spices around 6 months, once they’re developmentally ready for solids.


### Are herbs and spices safe for babies?


Yes. In small amounts, most herbs and spices are safe and can be a great way to gently introduce flavor early on.


### Do I need to wait between introducing different spices?


You don’t need long waiting periods. It’s helpful to introduce one new spice at a time and observe how your baby responds.


### Should I avoid any seasonings in the first year?


Yes. Avoid added salt, sugar, and salt-based seasoning blends like garlic salt or onion salt in the first year. Also, avoid anything too spicy or excessively seasoned.


### What are good first herbs and spices for babies?


Mild options like cinnamon, garlic, thyme, oregano, cumin, rosemary, and ginger are great places to start—especially if these are already used in your family meals.
